one_liner: Memory bandwidth and latency benchmark whose NEON, ARM and SSE2 copy/fill kernels beat old ARM libc memcpy up to 2.2x.
what_it_does: tinymembench is a single command-line program (main.c, util.c, asm-opt.c plus per-ISA .S files) that times sequential copy and fill over two 32 MiB aligned buffers and random-read latency over buffers up to 64 MiB. Each bandwidth row runs one kernel (libc memcpy/memset, C loops, NEON, VFP, ARM LDM/STM, SSE2, MOVSB/MOVSD, non-temporal and 2-pass variants with different prefetch steps) and prints the best MB/s of up to 10 runs of at least 0.5 s. It is a diagnostic tool, not a library: the kernels have the signature f(int64_t *dst, int64_t *src, int size) and no memcpy-compatible entry point.
how_it_is_fast: The faster rows use software prefetch a fixed 256 bytes ahead (pld on ARM, prefetchnta on x86, prfm on AArch64), wide NEON vld1/vst1 transfers of 32-128 bytes per iteration with 256-bit alignment hints, and non-temporal stores (movntdq, stnp) that skip the read-for-ownership of the destination. On 2012-2017 Cortex-A8 and Allwinner A13 boards the libc memcpy issued no prefetch, so a prefetching loop roughly doubled copy bandwidth; the 2-pass rows stage 2 KB blocks through L1 to test whether separating reads and writes helps.
when_to_use: Characterising a new ARM, AArch64, MIPS or x86 board: it shows in one run whether the system libc memcpy/memset reaches the memory bus's achievable bandwidth or leaves a 1.5-2x gap that a prefetching or NEON copy would close.

Choosing a copy strategy (prefetch distance, NEON vs LDM/STM, non-temporal vs cached stores) before writing or picking a memcpy for an embedded Linux image or a framebuffer driver; it also measures uncached framebuffer readback on ARM.
Comparing against the 68 community result pages on the project wiki, which use the same harness and output format across boards from the Raspberry Pi 1 to recent desktop CPUs.
Measuring random-access latency with and without transparent huge pages (MADV_HUGEPAGE) to see TLB costs.
when_not_to_use: As a memcpy or memset replacement: the kernels assume sizes in whole blocks and aligned pointers, have no small-copy, misalignment or overlap handling, and are not exported as a library.

Modern x86 with a current glibc: on the i7-8700T libc memcpy is within 4% of the best kernel (non-temporal copy) and on the Ryzen 9800X3D libc memcpy ties the best SSE2 copy, so there is nothing to copy across.
Machines whose last-level cache holds 64 MiB or more: the two 32 MiB buffers are fixed at compile time, so the 'memory bandwidth' rows measure cache bandwidth there (see gotchas).
Multi-threaded bandwidth: the program is single-threaded (multi-thread support is an open request, issue #22), so it understates total DRAM bandwidth on multi-core parts.
Clang or MSVC toolchains: clang fails to assemble the .S files (issue #20, open), and Windows builds go only through mingw/msys (Win64 via mingw64 since 2017-02-13).

integration.form: source-drop (standalone benchmark program built with make)
integration.dependencies: libc and libm; Linux /dev/fb0 optional for framebuffer tests
integration.min_toolchain: GCC with GNU as (C89-style C plus GNU assembler macros); clang assembly fails per issue #20
integration.platforms: x86 and x86-64 (SSE2; Linux and mingw Win64), 32-bit ARM (ARMv4 to ARMv7, VFP, NEON), AArch64, MIPS32
integration.thread_safety: single-threaded benchmark; not applicable as a library

gotchas: Harness flaw on large-cache CPUs: main.c fixes the buffers at #define SIZE (32 * 1024 * 1024) with no compile-time override (unlike MAXREPEATS), so src plus dst is 64 MiB. The Ryzen 7 9800X3D has 96 MB of L3, and its wiki page reports libc memcpy at 81381.2 MB/s copied (about 163 GB/s of read plus write traffic) and memset at 156460.7 MB/s, both above the 96 GB/s peak of the page's dual-channel DDR5-6000 (derived from page data). That page measures L3, not DRAM, and its 'non-temporal copy 2.5x slower than libc' result reflects non-temporal stores going to DRAM while cached copies stay in L3, not a general verdict on modern x86.

C-kernel rows are compiler-sensitive: issue #7 showed forward and backward C copies swapping 3.5-4x between gcc 4.6.3 and 4.7.2 on a Cortex-A7, and store order was only forced with volatile on 2016-03-29 (v0.4). The Allwinner A13 run (v0.2.9) and the Raspberry Pi runs (v0.3.9) predate that fix, and no wiki page records compiler, flags or libc version, so cite the NEON/ARM assembly rows rather than the C rows.

Kernels are not safe on arbitrary input: loops are do-while style (subs/jg), so size 0 still writes one block; sizes are processed in 32, 64 or 128-byte steps and the NEON unrolled copy rounds size down with bic #127, silently dropping a tail; NEON stores carry :256 alignment hints and SSE2 uses movdqa, which fault on unaligned pointers; the non-temporal SSE2 kernels end without sfence.

Baselines vary per page: the overclocked Raspberry Pi run on a custom 4.1.15 kernel shows libc memcpy at 307.9 MB/s, below the stock run's 387.6 MB/s despite higher clocks, so the libc (or preloaded copy routines) differed between runs on the same page; issue #30 (open) reports a segfault in aligned_block_copy_movsb under MSYS2 gcc 13.3 on Windows.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick tinymembench to diagnose whether a board's libc copy is leaving bandwidth on the table; to actually ship faster copies, use a packaged replacement such as copies-and-fills (libcofi_rpi) or arm-mem on 32-bit ARM, or Arm Optimized Routines on AArch64. rvv-bench plays the same benchmark-program role for RISC-V Vector boards, which tinymembench does not support (RISC-V is an open request, issue #31).
verified_claims_summary: Community wiki runs of the project's own harness (best MB/s over 32 MiB aligned buffers, compiler, flags and libc not recorded) show NEON prefetched copy at 563.5 MB/s against 258.3 MB/s for libc memcpy on a 1 GHz Cortex-A8 BeagleBone Black (2.18x) and NEON unrolled copy at 499.9 vs 249.8 MB/s on an Allwinner A13 (2.0x). Libc memset ties every custom fill on those ARM boards; on x86 the only gains are 1.04x (non-temporal copy) and 1.25x (non-temporal fill) on an i7-8700T, and on the Ryzen 9800X3D libc ties in a run that fits in L3.
status_note: Abandoned since 2017-02-14 (71 commits, 418 stars, 102 forks, 12 open issues, 9 open PRs) but MIT-licensed, small and still used: the wiki keeps receiving runs from current CPUs; build with GCC and treat the numbers as diagnostics, not as a library recommendation.
